A drone manufacturing facility in Kyiv was destroyed in a Russian ballistic missile strike on Friday. According to reports, the factory was owned by Terminal Autonomy, a U.S.-registered company incorporated in Delaware, marking what has been described as the first reported strike on a U.S.-owned company during the conflict.

Former U.S. intelligence official Anthony Vinci said ownership of a manufacturing facility is unlikely to influence Russian targeting decisions if the site is considered to have military significance.
The strike comes amid continued debate over expanding defense production in Ukraine. Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States would authorize licensed production of Patriot air-defense missiles in Ukraine. 🔔 Ethereum price faces $2,000 test as oil surge revives rate fears 

⚡️ Ethereum price has remained trapped below $2,000 as rising oil prices, renewed interest-rate concerns and BitMEX’s planned shutdown have tempered bullish sentiment despite continued spot ETF inflows. According to data from cryptonews, Ethereum price traded near $1,927 on July 23 after reaching an intraday high of $1,941. The token has recovered more than 27% from its June low near $1,514, but repeated failures around $1,955 have kept the psychological $2,000 level beyond buyers’ reach.

🔗 Rate traders have already adjusted their positions. The probability of a September Fed hike rose to 79% from 68% per data from the CME FedWatch tool. Expectations for the July meeting remain centered on no change, but another oil-led inflation increase could lift Treasury yields and pressure risk assets such as Ethereum. 

🔖 U.S. equities also weakened after Alphabet raised its 2026 capital-spending forecast to between $195 billion and $205 billion. The company recorded negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion as quarterly expenditure doubled to $44.9 billion, while its shares fell in premarket trading.

The Patriot Passport: Now With 250,000 Limited Editions

The State Department announced that a commemorative passport featuring Trump leaning over the Resolute Desk will finally go national on August 8, after 250,000 copies were previously rationed out of a single office in Washington, Forbes reports. 

It won't replace the standard passport, it's optional, it's scarce, and it's numbered like a trading card. Nothing says national unity like a limited-edition government document with a face on it.

Some travelers weren't thrilled to discover the president might end up in their carry-on by default. 

A tip circulating on Reddit advised applicants at the Washington Passport Agency to specifically request the large-format 52-page book if they wanted to dodge the commemorative design, a workaround that exists only because enough people assumed the presidential edition would simply become the new normal. 

It says something that the State Department needed users to crowdsource an opt-out.

This is not, notably, a one-off. Trump's portrait already went up on National Parks passes earlier this year, administration officials have floated putting his face and signature on a new $250 bill, and his name was slapped onto the Kennedy Center signage before a federal judge ordered it removed for lacking congressional approval. 

The passport is just the latest entry in a slow-motion rebrand of federal paperwork into merchandise, one office, one bill denomination, one building at a time.

None of this requires anyone's vote or a line in a budget bill, just a printing order and a signature the office already has on file. 

If the presidency can restyle a passport, a park pass, and eventually maybe a $250 bill without asking anyone, what exactly is left that still needs an act of Congress?
